children: The European Union's top official said Brussels has plans to stop children under 13 from accessing social networks and restrict what teenagers can do online.

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission's president, on Wednesday revealed details of a plan for a new EU-wide law curbing minors' access to social networks as more countries in the bloc have started work on their own rulebooks.

Under the plans, children under 13 wouldn't have access to social media, while those between 13 and 15 would get limited access under parental supervision, and online platforms would be obliged to ensure they are safe for young people older than that, according to von der Leyen.

Governments worldwide have turned to social media bans amid outcry from parents and campaigners. Von der Leyen cited concerns linked to children's mental health including loss of sleep and self-harm during a speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg where she laid out the plan on Wednesday.

"Children are pulled ever deeper into feeds designed to keep them scrolling," she told EU lawmakers. "What we are witnessing is a great capture of our children. A capture of their attention, their focus, their minds," she said.
The commission plans to propose a so-called Kids Act this week, which would govern young people's access to platforms.

Australia became the first country to enforce a social media ban for under 16s in 2025. Florida has also introduced restrictions for under 14s in the U.S., while several EU countries including France, Greece, and Spain have also sought to bring in restrictions.

The EU's executive arm has itself moved to work on a rulebook that would cover the 27-member bloc. A panel of experts--convened by Von der Leyen--issued a report earlier this year outlining how they believe rules should be implemented, including by staggering how children can use platforms as they grow up.
Von der Leyen said the EU would take a gradual approach with tailored protection levels.
"Each age has its own sensitivities, and therefore each will have its own tailored protection level," she said.

The details of the social media plan came as part of a broader speech to lawmakers where the EU chief also touched on simplifying the bloc's knot of regulations, climate, critical raw materials, artificial intelligence risks and relations with China.
